steps: Separate voice from tone: write 3 to 4 voice traits that never change, each as 'we are X, not Y', and a table of tone shifts by situation (celebrating, onboarding, apologising, warning). Mailchimp's own split is the pattern: voice constant, tone varies.
For each piece, name the reader's state of mind first (relieved, confused, anxious, excited) and set the tone from it. An error message and a launch email do not share a tone, only a voice.
Plain-English pass: active voice, everyday words, no slang or B2B jargon, positive phrasing ('To get a refund, send the order ID', not 'You can't get a refund without the order ID').
Clarity over cleverness: read each joke and delete it if it competes with the instruction or the offer.

Mechanics pass (the guide's choices, adjust to the client): contractions allowed, serial comma, numerals except at the start of a sentence, spelled-out dates, % symbol, hyphen for ranges, one exclamation mark at most and none in errors, emoji used rarely and on purpose, lowercase 'email' and 'internet'.

Accessibility pass: descriptive link text, headings nested in order, real lists, alt text on images, abbreviations explained on first use, captions or transcripts for video (edit:accessible_writing_check).
Writing about people: check how the copy refers to customers, disabilities, gender and identity against the guide's section; apply inclusive wording (edit:inclusive_language).
Translation: avoid idioms and puns that will not travel; for Hinglish or Hindi versions use transcreation, not word-for-word (lang:transcreation).

Build the client guide: copy the section list as a skeleton, fill each with the client's decisions, add a word list, keep it short enough to be used. Test it by having a second writer draft from it and comparing results (edit:brand_voice_audit).

Does each piece state the reader's likely state of mind and match its tone to it?
Is every joke secondary to the clarity of the message?
Is there at most one exclamation mark, and none in an error or failure message?
Are abbreviations explained on first use and links descriptive?
Is language inclusive and free of jargon and slang?
Do spelling and mechanics match the client's recorded variant?

cards.name: Microsoft Writing Style Guide
cards.summary: Microsoft's free tech-writing and UI style reference: warm, crisp, conversational, contractions, sentence-case headings, bias-free and global English. Its 'Top 10 tips' page is a one-page edit checklist: bigger ideas with fewer words, write like you speak, get to the point fast, be brief, sentence case, minimal punctuation in titles, serial comma, one space after periods, start with a verb.
use_for: UI text, product copy, help articles and onboarding flows (genre:ux_microcopy, genre:knowledge_base_article)
SaaS and tech marketing copy that must sound human and brief
global audiences and non-native readers (lang:global_plain_english)
inclusive-language and bias-free checks
a one-page checklist when a client has no style guide
avoid: Contractions where the register is formal or legal: Microsoft uses them to sound friendly. Keep a legal notice or a condolence message uncontracted, as the brief's tone requires.
Mixing contractions and full forms in one UI: the guide says not to mix 'can't' and 'cannot' in the same UI.
Forming contractions from a noun and a verb ('Microsoft's developing...') or using awkward ones (there'd, it'll, they'd): the guide advises against them.
Cutting to the point of coldness: 'shorter is always better' is Microsoft's brand rule for its own products; keep what the user needs to decide.

sources.title: Microsoft Writing Style Guide: Top 10 tips for Microsoft style and voice
sources.supports: top 10 tips: bigger ideas fewer words; write like you speak; contractions; get to the point fast; be brief; sentence-style capitalisation; no period or colon at the end of headings; serial comma; one space after periods and no spaces around dashes; start with a verb and avoid 'there is'

sources.title: Microsoft Writing Style Guide: Use contractions
sources.supports: use common contractions; do not mix with spelled-out forms in UI text; never contract a noun and a verb; avoid awkward contractions

sources.title: Microsoft Writing Style Guide: Bias-free communication
sources.supports: bias-free communication: gender-neutral alternatives; avoid he or she in generic references; singular 'they' acceptable

sources.title: Microsoft Writing Style Guide
sources.supports: the guide's scope: voice, word choice, grammar, global communications, scannable content

steps: Voice pass: read the text aloud (Microsoft: write like you speak). Replace jargon and complex phrasing with what you would say to a colleague.

Brevity pass: for each paragraph ask what the reader needs to decide or do, keep that, and cut the rest. Microsoft's own example turns a long paragraph about a feature into a single sentence that leads with the benefit.
Front-load: lead with what matters most; put the keyword the reader scans for at the start of headings and buttons; make the next step obvious (tech:front_loading).

Contractions: use common ones (it's, you'll, you're, we're, let's, don't); do not mix them with the full form in the same piece; skip awkward ones (there'd, it'll, they'd); never contract noun plus verb.
Capitalisation: sentence style everywhere (capitalise the first word and proper nouns only). When in doubt, do not capitalise.
Punctuation: no period or colon at the end of titles, headings and UI titles; serial comma in lists of three or more; one space after a period; no spaces around an em dash.

Weak-writing pass: start statements with a verb where you can, cut 'you can' when it adds nothing, and remove 'there is', 'there are', 'there were'. ('You can access Office apps across your devices' becomes 'Access Office apps on all your devices'.)

Bias-free pass: swap gendered terms for neutral ones (chairperson, sales representative, workforce), avoid 'he or she' in generic references by using 'you', plural forms or a role, and use singular 'they' where you cannot rewrite (edit:inclusive_language).
Global pass: avoid idioms and culture-specific references; keep sentences short enough to translate; spell out abbreviations on first use (lang:global_plain_english).
Run `python pcw.py check draft.txt`, fix AI-tell warnings, and record any client override on the style sheet (edit:style_sheet).

Does each paragraph lead with what matters most and cut what the reader does not need?
Are contractions used consistently, with none awkward and none mixed with full forms?
Is capitalisation sentence style throughout?
Are there no end periods or colons on headings and titles?
Is there a serial comma and one space after periods?

cards.name: Project style sheet
cards.summary: A running list of the piece's or client's decisions (spellings, names, capitals, hyphenation, numbers, terms) that you apply everywhere and hand over with the work. The EFA lists preparing style sheets that guide consistency as a core part of copyediting.
use_for: every client job longer than one page or repeated weekly (blogs, newsletters, social calendars)
multi-writer teams, so each writer follows the same decisions
long documents: books, white papers, reports, scripts
Hindi, Hinglish and Indian-English work, where several spellings of the same word are valid
handing a recurring client to another writer without losing the voice
avoid: Keeping decisions in your head: the next edit, the next writer or the AI session will make a different choice. Write each decision down the first time you make it.
A sheet so long no one reads it: record decisions that came up, not the whole style guide. Link to the base guide (edit:style_ap, edit:style_chicago, edit:style_gov_uk) instead of copying it.
Undated, unowned decisions: log who decided and when, so a later contradiction can be resolved.
Applying the sheet only at the end: apply it during the copy edit and the QA pass, and check new terms against it as they appear.

sources.title: Editorial Freelancers Association: Editorial service definitions
sources.supports: copyeditors prepare the style sheets that guide consistency and accuracy across the manuscript

sources.title: UNC Writing Center: Editing and proofreading
sources.supports: patterns of error: note what you tend to get wrong and set up a check for it

steps: Start from what exists: gather the client's brand voice guide, past published pieces and any base guide they follow. Write at the top which base guide applies (AP, Chicago, GOV.UK, the client's own) and the date.

Open a one-page table with columns: item, decision, reason or source, date, who decided. Use a shared file the client can see. Group rows by type: spelling, names, capitalisation, hyphenation, numbers and dates, punctuation, terms and product names, banned words and claims, links and formatting.

Seed it with the decisions that always come up: English variant (UK, US or Indian English), serial comma yes or no, heading case, how numbers and money are written (Rs, rupee symbol, lakh and crore, 'Rs 5 crore' or 'Rs 5 Cr'), date format, how the brand name and product names are spelt and capitalised, and whether contractions are allowed (lang:indian_english, lang:india_locale_formats).

Hindi and Hinglish rows: script per piece (lang:hinglish_roman or lang:hinglish_devanagari), the spelling you use for common Hinglish words (for example 'karo' or 'kro'), the nukta and matra conventions, and which English words stay in English.

Log decisions as you read the draft, the first time each issue arises: write the term exactly as it will appear, the chosen form and why. Add the page or section where it first occurs, so you can check context later.
Apply it in the copy edit: search the text for each logged term and its variants, and make every instance match (edit:copy_edit). Update the sheet when you spot a new variant.
Re-check at the QA gate: read the sheet against the final text, especially names, numbers and banned words (edit:pre_publish_qa).
Send it to the client for approval with the first delivery, flag the decisions you made on your own, and ask them to confirm or change. A client correction becomes a new row, not a one-off fix.
Version and hand over: save as <client>_stylesheet_<date>, keep one live copy, and give it to the next writer or the next AI session before they draft (tech:consistent_terminology).

Is every decision recorded with a reason or source and a date?
Are English variant, number and money format, date format, brand and product names and serial-comma choice all present?
For Hindi or Hinglish work, are script, spelling conventions and kept English words recorded?
Does the final text match every row?
Has the client seen and approved the sheet?
Is there one live version, handed to the next writer?

cards.name: Verb and voice pass
cards.summary: Find passive constructions, hidden verbs (nominalisations such as 'make a decision') and weak verb-plus-adverb pairs, and rewrite them with strong active verbs. It is a review, not a ban: the passive is right when the actor is unknown or unimportant.
use_for: almost every draft: this is the highest-yield line-edit pass
government, legal, bank and corporate copy written in a heavy official register
AI-assisted drafts, which lean on abstract nouns and passive phrasing
service and policy copy where responsibility must be clear (who does what, by when)
apology and update emails that must own the problem
avoid: Banning the passive: GOV.UK allows it where the outcome matters more than the actor, or where it makes the writing more user-centred. Google's style guide says the same.
Inventing an actor where none matters ('Someone built the temple in 1600'): leave it passive.
Using the passive to dodge blame in an apology or crisis note ('mistakes were made'): name who did what and what happens next (genre:apology_statement, genre:crisis_statement).
Treating Yoast's 10% passive threshold as a standard: it is the vendor's own choice, based on its testing. Use it as a flag, not a rule.
Turning every sentence into 'We do X': rotate to 'You' or to the thing the reader cares about.

sources.title: GOV.UK: Use clear language
sources.supports: use the active voice: more direct, keeps sentences short; passive acceptable when the outcome matters more than the agent; '-ion' and '-ment' words lengthen sentences

sources.title: Google developer documentation style guide: Active voice versus passive voice
sources.supports: prefer active voice; passive acceptable when emphasising the object or when the actor is unknown or irrelevant

sources.title: Yoast SEO: Readability analysis
sources.supports: passive voice check; Yoast's threshold is 10% of sentences, based on its testing

sources.title: Nominalization (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: nominalisation: turning verbs into nouns, hiding the verb

sources.title: UNC Writing Center: Editing and proofreading
sources.supports: grammar checkers can flag passive voice but you must judge the result

steps: Set the scene: this pass comes after the structure is settled (edit:reverse_outline) and as part of the line edit (edit:line_edit). Work paragraph by paragraph.

Find passives: look for a form of 'be' (is, are, was, were, been, being, will be) followed by a past participle (sent, approved, verified), often with 'by'. In Hindi and Hinglish look for 'kiya gaya', 'bheja jayega', 'diya jaata hai' and similar. A tool such as Hemingway Editor or Yoast's passive check will flag them, but you decide.

For each passive ask: who does the action? If the actor is named ('by the committee'), move it to the front: 'The committee reviews your application'. If it is not named, decide who it is (we, you, the bank, the department) and name it.

Keep the passive when you choose it: the actor is unknown or unimportant ('Aadhaar numbers are masked in the export'), or the object is the topic of the paragraph. Note it as deliberate so the next editor does not change it.

Find hidden verbs: look for abstract nouns ending in -ion, -ment, -ance, -al, and light verbs like 'make', 'give', 'have', 'take', 'carry out', 'perform' ('make a decision', 'give consideration to', 'carry out an inspection'). Rewrite with the verb inside: decide, consider, inspect (tech:unhide_verbs).

Fix verb-plus-adverb pairs: replace the pair with one precise verb ('walk slowly' becomes 'stroll'; 'work quickly' becomes 'rush' or, better, give the time: 'finish in 2 days'). Where the adverb is a hedge (really, very, quite), delete it (tech:cut_qualifiers).

Cut weak openers: sentences that begin 'There is', 'There are', 'It is' + adjective + 'that', or 'The fact that' usually hide the real subject and verb. Start with the thing doing the work (tech:concrete_nouns_strong_verbs).
Check rhythm after rewriting: if every sentence now starts with 'We', rotate some to start with 'You' or with the reader's goal. If the paragraph became too clipped, join two short sentences.
Count: if more than about a tenth of the sentences are still passive, check each is deliberate (Yoast's threshold is 10%, a vendor choice).
Run `python pcw.py check draft.txt` for the automatic first pass (it flags AI vocabulary and filler phrases), then the `humanizer` skill on English text (edit:ai_tell_removal).
checks: Is every remaining passive a deliberate choice (actor unknown, unimportant, or the object is the topic)?
Are all responsibilities in the piece clear: can you tell who does what and by when?
Are buried verbs ('make a decision', 'give consideration to') turned back into verbs?
Are verb-plus-adverb pairs replaced by precise verbs or numbers?
Do no more than two sentences in a row start with 'We' or 'There is'?
Do apologies and crisis lines name the actor and the action?
Did the pass keep the facts and meaning unchanged?

The thresholds are the vendor's choices, not standards: Yoast itself says the assessments are guidance, not a hard requirement.

a quick structural flag on long articles before the final read
teaching junior writers sentence and paragraph discipline
client reports where a readability traffic light is expected
Hindi and other languages where the passive and transition checks are supported (check Yoast's language list)
avoid: Chasing green lights: Yoast states a score does not guarantee rankings and that you do not need to fix every flag. Fix what a real reader would notice.
Forcing a transition word into every sentence: Yoast says there is no need, only enough to keep the logic flowing.
Trusting English-only checks on other languages: Yoast says Flesch Reading Ease and word complexity are English-only; passive voice and transition words support many languages.
Treating passive voice as an error: Yoast notes some sentences read better in the passive and some paragraphs must run long.
Skipping the human read: the tool cannot judge voice, accuracy or whether the hook works.

sources.supports: list of assessments (subheading distribution, paragraph length, sentence length, consecutive sentences, passive voice, transition words, text presence, word complexity, text alignment); passive threshold is 10% of sentences; Flesch and word complexity English-only; assessments are guidance; no ranking guarantee

steps: Set the language: choose the correct content language in Yoast so the right checks run. Check Yoast's language-support list before trusting results in Hindi or any non-English text; word complexity and Flesch scores are English-only.
Draft first, check second: finish the content and the structure (edit:reverse_outline) before reading the traffic lights, so you do not edit to the tool while still writing.
Passive voice: read the flagged sentences. Rewrite those where the actor matters; keep those where the passive is the better sentence. Yoast's 10% of sentences is its own threshold (edit:verb_pass).

Sentence length and paragraph length: split the flagged sentences at natural seams and break long paragraphs at the change of idea (edit:sentence_length_audit). Do not break a paragraph in the middle of an idea just to clear the flag.

Subheading distribution: if a long stretch has no subheading, add a descriptive one that tells the skimmer what that section contains (tech:descriptive_subheads, edit:seo_on_page). Do not add empty headings to satisfy the check.

Transition words: where the logic needs a signpost ('however', 'therefore', 'for example'), add one; if the sentences already flow, leave them. There is no need for one in every sentence (Yoast's own FAQ).
Consecutive sentences: if several sentences in a row start the same way, vary the openers or merge two (tech:transitions).
Word complexity (Premium, English only): replace the flagged jargon with plain words, unless the term is needed and explained.
Stop when the remaining flags are ones you can defend: keep a short note ('passive kept: actor unimportant'), and move to the human passes (edit:line_edit, edit:proofread).
Then run `python pcw.py check draft.txt` and, for English, the humanizer skill: the checks Yoast lists do not cover AI tells.
checks: Was the correct language set and its support confirmed for the checks you rely on?
Are remaining passive, long-sentence and long-paragraph flags each defensible?
Does every long section have a descriptive subheading?
Are transition words used where the logic needs them, not forced into every sentence?
Do consecutive sentences vary their openers?
Were Hindi and Hinglish passages checked by a human, since English-only checks do not apply?
Was the draft also checked for voice, facts and AI tells, which Yoast does not cover?
